claims.text: Incorporating silicon into a boride-based component will improve its resistance to corrosion by molten aluminum.
A silicon addition of approximately 5 wt% is an appropriate target for the intervention.
Silicon can be introduced effectively either by alloying or by a reactive surface treatment during processing.
Silicon will oxidize during exposure and form a continuous, adherent, Si-rich, likely SiO2-based surface layer.
The Si-rich surface layer will act as a barrier to penetration by molten aluminum.
Silicon promotes rapid oxidation and formation of a passivating SiO2-rich film during immersion in molten aluminum.
The passivating film minimizes contact between molten aluminum and the underlying boride matrix.
Reduced contact between molten aluminum and the boride matrix significantly lowers the corrosion rate relative to an undoped component.
Silicon-doped components will show lower weight loss than undoped components under identical hot-dip conditions.
Silicon-doped components will show less surface degradation than undoped components under identical hot-dip conditions.
The intervention should remain effective in molten aluminum at approximately 660°C and up to approximately 700°C.
Effectiveness depends on the temperature remaining within the stability range of the passivating film.
Sufficient environmental oxygen is required to form the proposed SiO2 layer.
Excess silicon or processing variations might adversely affect the component's mechanical properties.
